name: OTH_meyniel_cop_number_sqrt_n
title: Meyniel's conjecture on the cop number
statement_text: There is an absolute constant $C$ such that every connected graph $G$ on $n$ vertices has cop number $c(G) \le C\sqrt{n}$.
context_text: In the game of Cops and Robbers, $k$ cops choose vertices, then the robber chooses a vertex, and the two sides alternate moves (cops first), each piece moving to a vertex at distance at most one; the cops win if a cop occupies the robber's vertex. The cop number $c(G)$ is the least $k$ for which the cops have a winning strategy. Writing $c(n)$ for the maximum of $c(G)$ over connected graphs of order $n$, the conjecture says $c(n) = O(\sqrt{n})$; it is equivalent to $M_k = \Omega(k^2)$, where $M_k$ is the minimum order of a connected graph with cop number $k$ (Baird et al. 2014). The bound would be tight up to the constant: incidence graphs of projective planes give $c(n) \ge \sqrt{n/2} - o(\sqrt n)$.

related.note: cop number vs. treedepth, from the paper proving $c(G) \le k/2^{(1-o(1))\sqrt{\log k}}$ for vertex cover number $k$
sharpness of the high-girth lower bound $\Omega((\delta-1)^{g/4})$

notes: Stated by Meyniel in a 1985 personal communication to Frankl and first published in P. Frankl, 'Cops and robbers in graphs with large girth and Cayley graphs', Discrete Appl. Math. 17 (1987). Not in the corpus before this record: Open Problem Garden has no Cops and Robbers page, so the candidate OPG cross-links that the fuzzy matcher proposed for the arXiv-extracted records citing this conjecture were all refused in triage (they carry `manual_rejected` in data/arxiv_opg_matches.json). Those arXiv records remain in the corpus; only the link to an OPG page was withheld, because no such page exists. The workstream approaches the conjecture from the disproof side (what a counterexample would have to look like).

source.title: problems/meyniels_conjecture — self-contained workstream in this repository
source.reference: P. Frankl, Cops and robbers in graphs with large girth and Cayley graphs, Discrete Applied Mathematics 17 (1987) 301–305

name: OTH_bermond_lobsters_graceful
title: Graceful Lobster Conjecture
statement_text: Every lobster is graceful: if $T$ is a lobster with $m$ edges, there is an injective labeling $f\colon V(T)\to\{0,1,\dots,m\}$ such that $\{|f(u)-f(v)| : uv\in E(T)\} = \{1,2,\dots,m\}$.
context_text: A caterpillar is a tree whose non-leaf vertices induce a path; a lobster is a tree that becomes a caterpillar after all its leaves are deleted. Caterpillars are graceful (Rosa 1967), so lobsters are the natural next class towards the Graceful Tree Conjecture (Ringel–Kotzig), of which this conjecture is a special case. Known partial results include lobsters with a perfect matching (Morgan 2002), all trees of diameter at most 5 (Hrnčiar and Haviar 2001), and many families defined by the numbers of branches at the spine vertices (Wang, Jin, Lu and Zhang 1994; Mishra and coauthors 2010–2017; Superdock 2013). Krop (arXiv:1402.3994; Bull. Inst. Combin. Appl. 74 (2015)) claims the case of lobsters with an almost perfect matching. Every tree with at most 35 vertices is graceful (Fang, arXiv:1003.3045), so small cases carry no information on the conjecture.

related.note: the Graceful Tree Conjecture (all trees are graceful), which contains this conjecture as the special case of lobsters

notes: Stated in J.-C. Bermond, 'Graceful graphs, radio antennae and French windmills' (1979), and listed as open in Gallian's dynamic survey of graph labeling. Not in the corpus before this record: Open Problem Garden has only the general Graceful Tree Conjecture, the arXiv extraction has no lobster-gracefulness record, and the Bondy–Murty appendix does not list it. Added on request (issue #25), without a workstream in this repository.

source.title: J. A. Gallian, A dynamic survey of graph labeling, Electron. J. Combin. DS6 (lists the conjecture as open)
source.reference: J.-C. Bermond, Graceful graphs, radio antennae and French windmills, in Graph Theory and Combinatorics (Milton Keynes, 1978), Research Notes in Math. 34, Pitman, London, 1979, 18–37
